title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain
openingText: You don’t know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain’t no matter. That book was made by Mr. Mark Twain, and he told the truth, mainly. There was things which he stretched, but mainly he told the truth. That is nothing. I never seen anybody but lied one time or another, without it was Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary.
about:
Huckleberry Finn, a boy from a small Missouri river town, tells his own story. He runs away from a violent father and from the widow who is trying to civilise him, and he joins Jim, an enslaved man who has also run away. They drift down the Mississippi on a raft, meeting con men, feuding families, mobs and a few kind people.

Mark Twain wrote the book in several regional dialects, which he lists in his “Explanatory” note, and the English text keeps them. **The book uses racial slurs and presents slavery from the point of view of a boy who has been taught to accept it.** Both the English and the Danish editions keep the original word of the period, written as it was in the source; replacing it would be an editorial decision for the owner.

whyItMatters.title: A boy’s conscience against his teaching
whyItMatters.body: Huck has been told that helping Jim escape is a sin and a theft. The novel shows him deciding against what he has been taught, though he thinks he is choosing wrongly. The book lets a reader watch the gap between a law and a person’s conscience.

whyItMatters.title: A narrator who does not see everything
whyItMatters.body: Huck reports what he sees without judging it, so the reader must notice what he misses. The humor and the horror both come from that distance. Few other novels use a young narrator so effectively.

whyItMatters.title: The river as a road
whyItMatters.body: The raft carries the story from town to town and shows many kinds of American life. The river is also where Huck and Jim are freest. Twain’s descriptions of dawn and storm on the Mississippi are among the best parts of the book.

angleCards.title: Follow Huck’s conscience
angleCards.text: Mark each moment when Huck weighs what he was taught against what he sees in Jim.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Adventures of Huckleberry Finn to follow how Huck’s conscience changes.

angleCards.title: Read the dialects
angleCards.text: Notice how Twain’s listed dialects mark who is speaking and where they come from.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Adventures of Huckleberry Finn to see how dialect shapes character and place.

angleCards.title: Watch the con men
angleCards.text: Track the Duke and the King and ask what each trick shows about the towns they fool.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Adventures of Huckleberry Finn to understand what the con men reveal about the society around them.

angleCards.title: Question the ending
angleCards.text: Read the last chapters and ask what Tom’s games do to Jim and to the story’s meaning.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Adventures of Huckleberry Finn to judge how the ending fits with the rest of the novel.
